To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the KGF EAS array has been used to search for gamma ray emission from point sources in the 10-1000 TeV region.
we have searched for gamma ray sources in the energy range 0.5 to 10 GeV and we found no evidence for point source emission.
the KGF array is sensitive to UHE gamma rays from Cyg X3 and Her X1 and we have set upper limits on the long term gamma ray flux from these sources.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the search for point sources of UHE gamma rays in the northern sky.
the study of high energy cosmic ray showers and their applications to astrophysics.

the following: (1) The study of the energy spectrum of cosmic rays up to energies of 1000 TeV, (2) the search for gamma rays from astrophysical objects, (3) the search for point sources of cosmic rays and gamma rays, and (4) the search for the time variations of the cosmic ray intensity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
no significant emission of EAS from the sky was detected by the KGF array.
the KGF experiment has not observed any point sources of UHE gamma rays.
no point sources have been detected with a significance level of 5σ.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the flux of UHE gamma rays from Cyg X3 is less than (0.5-1.5) x 10 ^{-11} cm ^{-2} sec ^{-1} in the energy range 2-10 ^{14} eV, and from Her X-1 is less than 0.5-2 x 10 ^{(11)} cm ^{-2 sec ^{-1}} for the same energy range.
the upper limits for point sources are in general better than the limits from other experiments.
there is no evidence for any significant gamma ray emission from any known galactic sources.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the EAS technique is sensitive to gamma rays with energies up to a few TeV.
we can see the Crab Nebula in gamma rays with a significance of 3 sigma, and we have set a limit of 1% on the flux of gamma rays with energies > 100 GeV from Cygnus X-3.
we are sensitive to the emission from the Crab Nebula and the Crab pulsar.
